October 1, 2026

Hegseth announces purge of 20% of top military officers

tags: defence, politics
sources: @aaronparnas, @hunteralexanderhowell

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced he will cut 20% of the United States military's top generals and flag officers, writing that the force wants "no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals, just warriors." He framed the cuts as removing what he called wokeism from the ranks, and paired them with an expanded push to integrate artificial intelligence into the military. Critics said removing a fifth of senior leadership would have severe consequences for the armed forces, and questioned the exclusion of "radicals" given Hegseth's own advocacy for striking Iran.

Justice Department accused of withholding Epstein banker interview

tags: politics, legal
sources: @aaronparnas

Senator Ron Wyden has written to the Justice Department demanding an FBI 302 memorializing an interview with a banker linked to Jeffrey Epstein, which was left out of the files released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act. The letter argues the document's exclusion suggests other 302s are also being withheld in violation of the law. Wyden indicated that if the document is not produced, Senate Democrats would subpoena it should they take the majority.

Commerce Department proposes counting only citizens and green card holders in 2030 census

tags: politics, immigration
sources: @groundnews

The Commerce Department has proposed apportioning the 435 House seats using only U.S. citizens and permanent residents, which would exclude an estimated 17 to 18 million people, about 5% of the population, including refugees, asylum seekers and visa holders. No census since 1790 has excluded non-citizens, and the 14th Amendment apportions seats by "the whole number of persons in each State." A second proposed change would remove race and ethnicity from the short form, which critics say would undercut Voting Rights Act litigation. Public comment on the rules closes October 13, and each change carries its own severability clause.

Tennessee halts executions after lethal injection attempt fails

tags: legal, politics
sources: @aaronparnas, @groundnews

Tennessee officials failed to execute Christa Gail Pike after administering two doses of pentobarbital, and Governor Bill Lee halted the state's remaining execution this year and ordered a third-party review. Pike, 50, remained alive after the injections and was taken by ambulance from Riverbend Maximum Security Institution to a hospital; her condition was not disclosed. Her attorneys cited difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital and the absence of emergency medical care, and said she reported burning pain. Pike was sentenced to death for a 1995 killing committed when she was 18 and would have been the state's first woman executed in at least 200 years.

USPS pilot puts scanning cameras in mail trucks

tags: surveillance, privacy
sources: @aaronparnas

The United States Postal Service is running a pilot program placing cameras inside mail carrier vehicles that continuously scan roads, signage and sidewalks, according to 404 Media. The agency describes the purpose as improving community safety, using the fleet's constant nationwide movement as a data collection network. The cameras will not record audio. Privacy advocates have objected to the scope of the collection.

Federal government auto-enrolls children into consolidated "Trump accounts" database

tags: privacy, surveillance
sources: @total.hypocrisy

Tens of millions of children and their families are being auto-enrolled starting October 1, 2026 into federally administered savings accounts presented as a nest egg available at age 18. Opening the accounts requires a child's name, Social Security number, guardian identity, addresses updated over time and potentially passport information. The concern raised is that records currently siloed across the Social Security Administration, the State Department and other agencies are being merged into a single profile accessible to federal personnel or to anyone who breaches it.

Pentagon breach exposes data on 2.76 million military personnel

tags: surveillance, defence
sources: @groundnews

A breach of the Pentagon's Defense Manpower Data Center exposed Social Security numbers and other personal information of current and former military and civilian personnel. Unauthorized users accessed a vulnerable server beginning last October, but the Pentagon did not discover and fix the problem until July. The breach affected 2.76 million living people and 294,000 deceased people, and the unencrypted data in some cases included military occupational specialties. The Pentagon said it has no indications of misuse, while security experts warned the data could be combined with commercial records to profile or target personnel.

Startup seeks 456 nuclear reactors on Utah public land to power data centers

tags: climate, tech
sources: @carolinegleich

Valor Atomics, a California startup founded in 2023 whose only reactor is a test unit in a tent-like structure in Emery County, has proposed Project Beehive: 456 reactors, data centers, a nuclear fuel plant and waste storage across 9,000 acres of public land near Price, Utah. The State Trust Lands Board unanimously approved 640 acres of state land on September 17, and the federal land is under review. The power would serve data centers rather than the grid. Opponents point to the region's history of atomic testing fallout and uranium milling, the cancelled $9 billion small modular reactor project backed by Utah cities in 2023, the absence of any permanent waste repository, and unresolved questions about cooling water in one of the driest states. County hearings and a federal comment period are expected.

Trump Justice Department reviews whether Nixon was treated unfairly over Watergate

tags: politics, legal
sources: @aaronparnas

The Justice Department has begun examining whether Richard Nixon was mistreated by the Watergate special prosecutor's office and whether that prosecution was politically motivated, according to the Wall Street Journal. Former Nixon aide Geoff Shepard was brought in to give a two-hour presentation laying out his theory that Nixon was taken down improperly. The review follows Trump asking Republicans why Nixon chose to resign rather than fight.

Cornell police statement on assault allegation never reached district attorney

tags: legal, media
sources: @aaronparnas

CBS News confirmed that a Jane Doe was interviewed by Cornell University campus police on November 14, telling them "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped" and that she was physically struck during the incident. The district attorney who declined to bring charges against seven fraternity members in 2014 told CBS he never saw the interview transcript and called it news to him. In her sworn statement she described extreme intoxication, being unable to reach her phone or arrange a ride, and fraternity members later bragging about what happened. A 2025 Cornell survey reported by WCAX found 35% of undergraduate women said they had been sexually assaulted on campus, and a journalist has publicly solicited information to unmask the Jane Doe.

Iranian court upholds 74 lashes for singer who performed without hijab

tags: politics, legal
sources: @groundnews

An Iranian appeals court upheld a sentence of 74 lashes for singer Parastoo Ahmadi over a December 2024 livestreamed concert in which she performed without the mandatory hijab, wearing a sleeveless dress. A criminal court convicted Ahmadi and eight members of her band and production team on charges including offending public decency, and barred them from audiovisual work and from leaving Iran for two years. Lawyers said the appeal was rejected without a hearing. Iranian law requires women to cover their hair and prohibits public performances by women.

Congress votes to end penny production after 234 years

tags: markets, politics
sources: @groundnews

The Senate passed the bipartisan Common Cents Act formally ending U.S. penny production, a year after the Mint stopped making the coin, and Trump is expected to sign it. The Mint says each penny costs almost 4 cents to produce and that ending production will save about $56 million a year; 3.2 billion were made in 2024. Pennies remain legal currency, but businesses may round cash transactions to the nearest 5 cents as supplies decline. The bill also permits zinc to replace some copper in nickels.

Air Force major faces court-martial over uniformed protest against Trump

tags: legal, defence
sources: @oafnation_actual

An Article 32 hearing officer has recommended a general court-martial for Air Force Maj. Jason Watson, who protested President Trump while in uniform at the Capitol. Several other allegations against him were recommended for dismissal. The convening authority has yet to decide whether the case goes to trial.

FBI and Philadelphia police begin new forensic search of home tied to seven missing women

tags: legal
sources: @oafnation_actual

Seven women are linked to a Philadelphia home where investigators recovered more than one million images and videos. The FBI and city police are starting a new forensic search of the property that will include removing portions of flooring, drywall and plaster.

82nd Airborne major sentenced to 17 months for domestic violence

tags: legal, defence
sources: @oafnation_actual

Maj. Isaac Gutierrez of the 82nd Airborne Division was sentenced to 17 months in prison after pleading guilty to domestic violence and communicating a threat. The Army says Gutierrez, a West Point graduate with a Ranger tab, held his wife at gunpoint and threatened to kill her during an hour-long argument at their Fort Bragg home.

Three charged in racially motivated attack on Marines near Oceanside Pier

tags: legal
sources: @oafnation_actual

One man has pleaded guilty and two others face federal hate-crime charges over what prosecutors describe as a violent attack on two Marines near Oceanside Pier. One Marine suffered a concussion, an orbital fracture, a sinus fracture and a fractured cheekbone.

Former Dover airmen sentenced to 189 months for phishing scheme

tags: legal
sources: @oafnation_actual

Two former Air Force members stationed at Dover Air Force Base were sentenced to a combined 189 months in federal prison. Prosecutors say their phishing scheme diverted more than $1.68 million from an Iowa victim and more than $720,000 from an Ohio victim.

Marine Corps hostile fire pay doubles to $450 a month

tags: defence
sources: @oafnation_actual

Marine Corps Hostile Fire Pay rose from $225 to $450 per month effective today. Imminent Danger Pay also increased to $275 per month, or $9.16 per qualifying day. The new rates apply across the Marine Corps Total Force, and eligibility rules are unchanged.

Sailors aboard USS Abraham Lincoln describe shortages on extended deployment

tags: defence
sources: @oafnation_actual

Sailors and Marines aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln told visiting lawmakers about difficulties with laundry, medicine, health care and obtaining enough food during the ship's extended deployment.

Army barracks guide directs NCOs to watch for signs of distress

tags: defence, health
sources: @oafnation_actual

A new Army barracks inspection guide instructs non-commissioned officers to take note of blackout curtains, bare walls and sudden changes in a soldier's weight or mood during checks.

Hegseth previews stripped-down military fitness test

tags: defence
sources: @oafnation_actual

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said a future physical fitness test across the services will require only a stopwatch and a clipboard, adding that no mobile gym would be needed. The specific events and implementation details have not been released.

Man subjects seized license plate reader to looping plate footage

tags: surveillance, privacy
sources: @aaronparnas

A man removed a Flock automated license plate reader camera and placed it in front of monitors feeding it an estimated 23,000 license plates per second. Footage of the stunt circulated widely online, drawing attention to the scale of data the cameras collect.

Trump says only Hispanics could survive a fall from new ballroom

tags: politics
sources: @aaronparnas

Speaking during a Hispanic Heritage Month event while showing guests a tunnel leading to a planned White House ballroom, which he described as also being a military complex with a drone port on top, Trump warned visitors not to fall over the edge and said "only Hispanic could survive that fall." The remark drew widespread criticism as racist.
